docs.title: About
docs.text:
A little about me

My name is Robert.

I’ve been teaching English and Polish for over seven years in Poland, Spain and Japan. I’ve also had a successful career in finance and IT, but languages are the thing I keep coming back to — because I genuinely love them.

I’ve also lived in Denmark, Germany, France, Czechia, Greece, Brazil and, of course, Poland and the UK. And as of 2025, I’ve travelled to exactly 100 countries.

I speak Polish, English and Spanish fluently, I’m highly proficient in French, German and Portuguese, and I can also communicate in Swedish, Russian and Czech. I’ve studied some Chinese and Thai, too.

That mix has taught me a lot about what really makes languages difficult: not just grammar, but sounds, sentence structure, habits of expression and the cultural logic behind the way people communicate.

When we work together, I don’t want to keep you inside a textbook bubble. We use real material: videos, interviews, social media, articles, everyday conversations and whatever else fits your interests and goals. I want you to hear how people actually speak, not just perfectly scripted dialogues recorded at half speed.

Our sessions are also a way to discover the country behind the language — its people, humour, habits, culture and everyday life. I choose content carefully according to your needs and interests, but the long-term goal is for you to start exploring on your own and find things you genuinely want to watch, read and listen to.

docs.title: Train Your Polish Like a Champ
docs.text:
My approach to language coaching is like training an athlete: we define a clear goal, break it into measurable milestones, practise consistently, analyse performance and adjust the training as you progress.

We do not waste valuable class time on things you can do effectively by yourself; instead, I give you relevant and interesting material to work with EVERY DAY over the week for just 10-15 minutes every day.

Each day, you send me a short text or voice message telling me what you read, watched or listened to, what you understood in Polish, what interested you and what you found difficult. I collect this language production over time, which allows me to see what you already have a strong grasp of, where patterns of difficulty are appearing and what we should work on next.

This also allows us to use spaced repetition—returning to important vocabulary and structures at carefully timed intervals—and retrieval practice, where you actively recall and use language rather than simply rereading or reviewing it. We also use deliberate practice: focused work on the specific skills that currently limit your performance, with immediate feedback and repeated opportunities to improve them.

Our classes therefore follow a clear flow: we review your engagement with Polish during the week, discuss what caught your interest, what you understood, what remained unclear and, most importantly, what you have begun to make your own. We then work directly on the areas you find most difficult—which I will often already have identified from your daily messages—before introducing new concepts, situations, dialogues, vocabulary and structures that build naturally on what you already know. You will be able to practice these area during your every day learning sessions during the week on your own while sending me your results.

Class time is particularly devoted to activities that benefit from a coach being present: conversation, pronunciation, correction, experimentation with new language and the kind of immediate feedback that is difficult to obtain when studying alone.

Throughout the process, I monitor engagement and progress, adjust the programme, set clear milestones and celebrate achievements, so that every week of practice moves you closer to the level of Polish you want to perform at.

docs.title: 10 practical classes for your first days in Poland
docs.text:
10 classes × 50 minutes

This crash course is designed for people arriving in Poland for holiday, a short stay, work, study, or to visit Polish family and friends. It focuses on the language you need from day one: reading signs, asking for help, ordering food, finding your way, using transport, shopping, checking in, and handling simple problems.

docs.title: What makes this course different?
docs.text:
• Builds pronunciation systematically: start with vowels and familiar consonants, then move to more challenging Polish sounds.
  • Anchors every lesson in a real-life situation.
  • Introduces grammar only when it becomes useful.
  • Emphasizes patterns and communicative chunks over memorizing tables.
  • Helps learners begin reading Polish immediately and use the language from the first class.

docs.title: Class 1 — First contact: reading Polish and asking for help
docs.text:
Situation: Your first moments in Poland: signs, approaching someone, communication problems, asking where something is, pointing directions

Phonetics: - vowels: a, e, i, o, u/ó, y, ą, ę - basic word stress

Grammar: - basic sentence patterns - yes/no questions - simple negation - useful expressions with the verb “to be”

docs.title: Class 2 — At a café
docs.text:
Situation: Ordering a drink or snack in a café

Phonetics: - pronunciation of ą and ę - voiced/voiceless consonant pairs - final devoicing

Grammar: - first exposure to the accusative case — biernik - feminine nouns as objects - useful prepositions - with/without expressions leading to instrumental and genitive

docs.title: Class 3 - Bus, tram and train
docs.text:
Situation: Finding the correct bus, tram, train, stop or platform.

Phonetics: - soft vs hard consonants, the use of letter i to denominate soft consonant - hard vs soft sound contrasts

Grammar: - yes/no questions - demonstratives - grammatical gender - movement “to” a destination - first exposure to the genitive case — dopełniacz after some prepositions

docs.title: Class 4 — Numbers, prices and time
docs.text:
Situation: Understanding prices, currency exchange rates.

Phonetics: - the role of i as vowel and softening signal - reading softened consonant combinations

Grammar: - noun forms after different numbers

docs.title: Class 5 — Shopping
docs.text:
Situation: Buying groceries and everyday items, paying at the till.

Phonetics:

Grammar: - quantity of things

docs.title: Class 6 — Restaurant Polish
docs.text:
Situation: Ordering a meal, answering questions, handling dietary needs.

Phonetics: - consolidation of sound contrasts - phrase stress and rhythm - pronunciation of longer restaurant vocabulary

Grammar: - accusative (biernik) review - instrumental (narzędnik) - genitive (dopełniacz) for “without” - preposition-dependent noun endings - basic present-tense verbs

docs.title: Class 7 — Hotel and accommodation
docs.text:
Situation: Checking in, asking about breakfast/Wi-Fi, reporting a problem.

Phonetics: - consonant clusters prz, trz, drz, szcz - breaking long words into sound groups - confident reading of unfamiliar words

Grammar: - high-frequency present verbs - expressing possession - positive and negative forms - jest / nie ma - infinitives - polite can/may/need expressions - genitive after negation

docs.title: Class 8 — Pharmacy, health and emergencies
docs.text:
Situation: Describing a health problem, asking for a pharmacy or doctor, reporting a loss.

Phonetics: - connected speech - final devoicing - voicing assimilation - why spoken Polish can sound different from spelling

Grammar: - describing pain and symptoms - genitive and accusative in common expressions - past tense introduction - masculine and feminine past endings - past forms reflecting speaker gender

docs.title: Class 9 — Visiting Polish family and friends
docs.text:
Situation: Meeting relatives and friends, accepting/refusing hospitality, joining simple conversations.

Phonetics: - full pronunciation review - oral vowels, ą, ę - voiced/voiceless consonants - hard/soft consonants - sibilant series, i, clusters, stress, connected speech

Grammar: - formal vs informal address - Pan/Pani vs informal forms - polite questions - conditional forms for polite requests - masculine/feminine forms - review of useful case patterns - review of present and past tense - recognition of common polite native-speaker forms

docs.title: Class 10 — Putting it all together
docs.text:
• Simple conversation in all above situations
  • Reading simple texts
  • Helpful resources: apps, website, etc. to help you while you are in Poland

docs.title: By the end of the course
docs.text:
You should be able to:

  • read unfamiliar Polish words with much greater confidence;
  • understand the main principles of Polish pronunciation;
  • recognise the most important Polish sound contrasts;
  • ask for help when communication becomes difficult;
  • order food and drinks;
  • ask for and understand basic directions;
  • use buses, trams and trains;
  • deal with essential numbers, prices and times;
  • shop and pay;
  • manage basic restaurant and hotel interactions;
  • communicate a simple health or practical problem;
  • participate more comfortably when visiting Polish family and friends;
  • recognise some of the most important Polish grammatical patterns rather than seeing changing word endings as completely unpredictable.

The emphasis throughout is on practical communication, confident pronunciation and understanding the patterns that make Polish easier to navigate.

docs.title: Polish Language Resources
docs.text:
Welcome!

This website is a growing reference for learners of Polish who can find resources in their own language. We are expanding the site to cover pronunciation, grammar and learning tools to for the speakers of English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese and Russian.

docs.title: The Polish Alphabet
docs.text:
The Polish alphabet is based on the Latin alphabet, but it contains 32 letters. In addition to omitting a few letters that are not used in Polish (Q, V, X), it also includes several letters unique to the Polish language.

The modern Polish alphabet is:

Aa Ąą Bb Cc Ćć Dd Ee Ęę Ff Gg Hh Ii Jj Kk Ll Łł Mm Nn Ńń Oo Óó Pp Rr Ss Śś Tt Uu Ww Yy Zz Źź Żż

The small hook beneath the letters ą and ę is called an ogonek (Polish for "little tail").

Besides single letters, Polish also has several digraphs (two letters representing a single sound):

ch, cz, dz, dź, dż, rz, sz

The letters Q, V, and X are not part of the Polish alphabet. They appear only in certain abbreviations (for example, V for volt, which is wolt in Polish) or in a few words of foreign origin (such as taxi and quiz).

docs.title: Stress
docs.text:
Unlike French, in Polish the stress falls on the penultimate (second-to-last) syllable in almost all cases.

The main exceptions, where the stress falls on the third syllable from the end, are:

  • Words of Greek origin ending in -ika and -yka (fizyka [ˈfʲizɨka])
  • Past-tense verbs with the endings -śmy and -ście (pytaliście [pɨˈtalʲiɕʨɛ] instead of [pɨtaˈlʲiɕʨɛ])
  • Conditional verbs with the endings -bym, -byś and -by (robiłbym [ˈrɔbʲiwbɨm] instead of [rɔˈbʲiwbɨm])
  • Numerals (czterysta [ˈʧtɛrɨsta] instead of [ʧtɛˈrɨsta])
  • Numerals followed by the suffix -kroć (tysiąckroć [ˈtɨɕɔnʦkrɔʨ] instead of [tɨˈɕɔnʦkrɔʨ])

There are also exceptions where the stress falls on the fourth syllable from the end:

  • Conditional verbs with the endings -byśmy and -byście (pisalibyśmy [pʲiˈsalʲibɨɕmɨ] instead of [pʲisalʲiˈbɨɕmɨ])
  • Past-tense verbs with the endings -żeśmy and -żeście (spytaliżeście [spɨˈtalʲiʒɛɕʨɛ] instead of [spɨtalʲiˈʒɛɕʨɛ])

docs.title: Vowels
docs.text:
Polish vowels are always pronounced short.

IPA Letter Written example Audio example English equivalent / approximation [a] a tak a as in father [ɛ] e krew e as in bed [i] i i ee as in see, but short [ɔ] o oko roughly the o in British English not [u] ó, u mówić, ku oo as in food, but short [ɨ] y syn No exact English equivalent. It is pronounced farther back than i, with the lips unrounded. [ɔ̃] ą mąż No direct English equivalent: a nasalized o [ɛ̃] ę język No direct English equivalent: a nasalized e

When spelling a word aloud, the letters a, e, i, and o are simply named after their respective sounds.

However, both ó and u are pronounced [u]. To distinguish them, they are called:

  • ó: u zamknięte ("closed u")
  • u: u otwarte ("open u")

Other names for ó are also commonly used:

  • o kreskowane ("crossed o")
  • o z kreską ("o with a stroke")

The choice between ó and u is largely etymological (based on the historical development of the word). As a result, confusing these two letters is one of the most common spelling mistakes in Polish.

The letter y is called igrek [ˈigrɛk] (borrowed from the French i grec). Among all Polish vowels, y is the only one that can never appear at the beginning of a word.

docs.title: The consonants and the letter i
docs.text:
In Polish, the letter i placed after a consonant palatalizes it (makes it “soft”).

When a vowel follows i, the i serves only to palatalize the consonant.

i before a vowel:

  • after the letters c, s, z, dz and n, it is not pronounced.
  • after other consonants, it is generally pronounced like [j].

Thus, the palatal consonants ć, ś, ź, dź and ń are written:

  • ć, ś, ź, dź, ń before a consonant or at the end of a word;
  • ci, si, zi, dzi, ni before a vowel.
Letters IPA Written example Audio example Notes bi [bʲ] biały pi [pʲ] piasek gi [gʲ] ogień ki [kʲ] cukier wi [wʲ] wiatr fi [fʲ] geografia di [dʲ] diabeł dzi [ʥ] dziad equivalent to dź ti [tʲ] sympatia ci [ʨ] ciasto equivalent to ć zi [ʑ] zielony equivalent to ź si [ɕ] siarka equivalent to ś hi [çʲ] hiena li [lʲ] afiliacja mi [mʲ] anatomia ni [ɲ] kuchnia equivalent to ń ria [rʲ] abituria

Note that soft consonants can never precede y, and hard consonants almost never precede i. (Exceptions: loanwords, for example dżinsy [ˈʤinsɨ] = jeans)

docs.title: Nasal vowels
docs.text:
The letters ę and ą are nasal vowels: ę is a nasal e and ą is a nasal o. Their pronunciation depends heavily on the consonants that follow them.

Letter Following consonant Written example IPA Audio example English equivalent ą f, w, h, ch, s, z, sz, ż, rz, ś, ź, end of word mąż [ɔ̃] No exact English equivalent; a nasalized o, similar to French on b, p skąpiec [ɔm] like om in Polish pompka g, k pociąg [ɔŋ] like on in Polish biedronka c, dz, d, t, cz, dż piątek [ɔn] on in Polish konto ć, dź bądź [ɔɲ] oń in Polish koń ę f, w, h, ch, s, z, sz, ż, rz, ś, ź język [ɛ̃] b, p gęba [ɛm] like em in Polish zemsta g, k dźwięk [ɛŋ] like en in Polish piosenka c, dz, d, t, cz, dż wędrować [ɛn] en in Polish ten ć, dź wszędzie [ɛɲ] eń in Polish pień end of word imię [ɛ] a regular Polish e

docs.title: “Simple” consonants
docs.text:
We first present the consonants that also exist in English. At the end of a word or before a voiceless consonant, voiced consonants that have a voiceless counterpart become their voiceless equivalents.

Letter Written example Audio example IPA English equivalent b bardzo [b] b in bed, b is never very plosive, the lips only touch chleb [p] p in pen, p is never very plosive, the lips only touch p pan d dom [d] d in dog, unlike in English, though, the tongue touches the teeth kod [t] t in top, unlike in English, though, the toungue touches the teeth t tak g góra [g] g in go katalog [k] k in key k kod w waga [v] v in very staw [f] f in fish f fala z za [z] z in zoo raz [s] s in see s sam j jajo [j] y in yes l lato [l] a clear/light l, with the tongue tip just behind the upper teeth and no raising of the back of the tongue m moment [m] m in man n noga [n] n in no ń koń [ɲ] similar to ny in canyon ł łuk [w] w in water

docs.title: Consonants with no exact equivalent in English
docs.text:
We now present consonants that do not have an exact equivalent in English. Here too, at the end of a word or before a voiceless consonant, voiced consonants that have a voiceless counterpart become their voiceless equivalents.

Letter Written example Audio example IPA Notes dz dzwon [dz] dz is close to ds in the English words adze or kids, but pronounced as a single movement. ksiądz [ts] c is close to ts in tsunami or to the German pronunciation of Zeit. It is the voiceless counterpart of dz. c cena ż, rz żaba, rzeka [ʒ] similar to s in English vision, but articulated farther back. The sound is darker and “thicker.” masaż, kalendarz [ʂ] similar to sh in English ship, but harder and articulated farther back in the mouth sz szef dż dżem [d͡ʒ] similar to j in English jam, but articulated slightly farther back cz czas [t͡ʂ]] similar to ch in English chair, but with the tongue slightly farther back in the mouth ź źle [ʑ] ź has no exact English equivalent; it is similar to s in vision, but softer and pronounced farther forward in the mouth. znaleźć [ɕ] ś is the voiceless counterpart of ź. It is similar to sh in English sheep, but softer and pronounced farther forward. ś świat dź dźwig [ʥ] dź is similar to j in English jeans, but softer and pronounced farther forward. miedź [ʨ] ć is the voiceless counterpart of dź. It is similar to ch in English cheese, but softer and pronounced farther forward in the mouth. ć ćma h, ch charakter, hotel [x] h and ch are pronounced the same way. English has no exact equivalent; the sound is similar to ch in Scottish loch or German Bach. It is produced as a stream of air at the back of the mouth, without vibrating the throat. r rdza [r] r is pronounced by vibrating the tip of the tongue just behind the upper teeth

Source: Wikibooks – Polnisch/Kurs/Phonetik (translated and adapted).

docs.title: L'alphabet polonais
docs.text:
L'alphabet polonais est basé sur l'alphabet latin, mais il compte 32 lettres. En plus de quelques lettres qui ne sont pas utilisées en polonais (Q, V, X), il comprend également plusieurs lettres propres à la langue polonaise.

L'alphabet polonais moderne est le suivant :

Aa Ąą Bb Cc Ćć Dd Ee Ęę Ff Gg Hh Ii Jj Kk Ll Łł Mm Nn Ńń Oo Óó Pp Rr Ss Śś Tt Uu Ww Yy Zz Źź Żż

Le petit crochet sous les lettres ą et ę s'appelle un ogonek (en polonais : « petite queue »).

Outre les lettres simples, le polonais possède également plusieurs digrammes (deux lettres représentant un seul son) :

ch, cz, dz, dź, dż, rz, sz

Les lettres Q, V et X ne font pas partie de l'alphabet polonais. Elles n'apparaissent que dans certaines abréviations (par exemple V pour volt, en polonais wolt) ou dans quelques mots d'origine étrangère (par exemple taxi, quiz).

docs.title: Accentuation
docs.text:
Contrairement au français, en polonais l’accent tonique tombe, dans (presque) tous les cas, sur l’avant-dernière syllabe.

Les exceptions, où l’accent tombe sur l’antépénultième syllabe (troisième à partir de la fin), sont :

  • Les emprunts d’origine grecque se terminant par -ika et -yka (fizyka [ˈfʲizɨka])
  • Les verbes au passé avec les désinences -śmy et -ście (pytaliście [pɨˈtalʲiɕʨɛ] au lieu de [pɨtaˈlʲiɕʨɛ])
  • Les verbes au conditionnel avec les désinences -bym, -byś et -by (robiłbym [ˈrɔbʲiwbɨm] au lieu de [rɔˈbʲiwbɨm])
  • Les numéraux (czterysta [ˈʧtɛrɨsta] au lieu de [ʧtɛˈrɨsta])
  • Les numéraux suivis du suffixe -kroć (tysiąckroć [ˈtɨɕɔnʦkrɔʨ] au lieu de [tɨˈɕɔnʦkrɔʨ])

Les exceptions, où l’accent tombe sur l’antéantépénultième syllabe (quatrième à partir de la fin), sont :

  • Les verbes au conditionnel avec les désinences -byśmy et -byście (pisalibyśmy [pʲiˈsalʲibɨɕmɨ] au lieu de [pʲisalʲiˈbɨɕmɨ])
  • Les verbes au passé avec les désinences -żeśmy et -żeście (spytaliżeście [spɨˈtalʲiʒɛɕʨɛ] au lieu de [spɨtalʲiˈʒɛɕʨɛ])

docs.title: Les voyelles
docs.text:
Les voyelles polonaises sont prononcées courtes.

API Lettre Exemple écrit Exemple audio Équivalent français [a] a tak a de chat [ɛ] e krew comme è dans mère [i] i i i de si [ɔ] o oko o de porte ou le o ouvert du sud de la France [u] ó, u mówić, ku ou de vous [ɨ] y syn Le y polonais est comme le e muet français, mais prononcé clairement dans "petit", se prononce plus en arrière que le i, tout en restant ouvert. [ɔ̃] ą mąż on de sont [ɛ̃] ę język ain dans main (prononciation québécoise)

Lorsqu’on épelle un mot, les lettres a, e, i et o sont simplement appelées comme leur son.

En revanche, les lettres ó et u se prononcent toutes les deux [u]. Pour les distinguer, on appelle :

  • ó : u zamknięte (« u fermé »)
  • u : u otwarte (« u ouvert »)

D’autres noms pour ó sont également utilisés :

  • o kreskowane (« o barré »)
  • o z kreską (« o avec un trait »)

Le choix entre ó et u est essentiellement étymologique (lié à l’histoire du mot). C’est pourquoi il s’agit d’une des fautes d’orthographe les plus fréquentes en polonais.

La lettre y est appelée igrek [ˈigrɛk] (du français i grec). Parmi toutes les voyelles polonaises, y est la seule qui ne peut jamais apparaître au début d’un mot.

docs.title: Les consonnes et la lettre i
docs.text:
En polonais, la lettre i placée après une consonne la palatalise (la rend « mouillée »).

Lorsqu'une voyelle suit le i, celui-ci ne sert qu'à palataliser la consonne.

Le i avant une voyelle:

  • après les lettres c, s, z, dz et n, ne se prononce pas.
  • après les autres consonnes, il se prononce généralement comme un [j].

Ainsi, les consonnes palatales ć, ś, ź, dź et ń s'écrivent :

  • ć, ś, ź, dź, ń devant une consonne ou à la fin d'un mot ;
  • ci, si, zi, dzi, ni devant une voyelle.
Lettres API Exemple écrit Exemple audio Remarques bi [bʲ] biały pi [pʲ] piasek gi [gʲ] ogień ki [kʲ] cukier wi [wʲ] wiatr fi [fʲ] geografia di [dʲ] diabeł dzi [ʥ] dziad équivalent à dź ti [tʲ] sympatia ci [ʨ] ciasto équivalent à ć zi [ʑ] zielony équivalent à ź si [ɕ] siarka équivalent à ś hi [çʲ] hiena li [lʲ] afiliacja mi [mʲ] anatomia ni [ɲ] kuchnia équivalent à ń ria [rʲ] abituria

Notez que les consonnes douces ne peuvent jamais précéder le y et que les consonnes dures ne précèdent presque jamais le i. (Exceptions: les emprunts lexicaux, par exemple dżinsy [ˈʤinsɨ] = jeans)

docs.title: Voyelles nasales
docs.text:
Les lettres ę et ą sont des voyelles nasales : ę est un e nasal et ą est un o nasal. Leur prononciation dépend fortement des consonnes qui les suivent.

Lettre Consonne suivante Exemple écrit API Exemple audio Équivalant français ą f, w, h, ch, s, z, sz, ż, rz, ś, ź, fin de mot mąż [ɔ̃] comme balcon en français b, p skąpiec [ɔm] comme om in pompka en polonais g, k pociąg [ɔŋ] comme on in biedronka en polonais c, dz, d, t, cz, dż piątek [ɔn] on de konto en polonais ć, dź bądź [ɔɲ] oń de koń en polonais ę f, w, h, ch, s, z, sz, ż, rz, ś, ź język [ɛ̃] b, p gęba [ɛm] comme em in zemsta en polonais g, k dźwięk [ɛŋ] comme en in piosenka en polonais c, dz, d, t, cz, dż wędrować [ɛn] en de ten en polonais ć, dź wszędzie [ɛɲ] eń de pień en polonais fin du mot imię [ɛ] un polonais régulier e

docs.title: Consonnes « simples »
docs.text:
On présente d'abord les consonnes qui existent en français. En fin de mot ou devant une consonne sourde, les consonnes sonores qui ont un équivalent sourd deviennent leurs équivalents sourds.

Lettre Exemple écrit Exemple audio API Équivalant français b bardzo [b] b de bas chleb [p] p de pas p pan d dom [d] d de dans kod [t] t de tu t tak g góra [g] g de grain katalog [k] c de comme k kod w waga [v] v de vache staw [f] f de fils f fala z za [z] z de zebra raz [s] s de fils s sam j jajo [j] y de yaourt l lato [l] l de lit m moment [m] m de main n noga [n] n de nom ń koń [ɲ] gn de cognac ł łuk [w] ou de oui

docs.title: Consonnes qui n'existent pas en français
docs.text:
On présente d'abord les consonnes qui n'existent pas en français. Ici, aussi, en fin de mot ou devant une consonne sourde, les consonnes sonores, qui ont un equivalant sourd, deviennent leurs équivalents sourds.

Lettre Exemple écrit Exemple audio API Rémarques dz dzwon [dz] dz est proche du ds dans l'anglais adze ou kids, mais prononcé d'un seul mouvement. ksiądz [ts] c est proche du ts dans tsunami ou dans la prononciation allemande de Zeit. Il est le correspondant sourd de dz. c cena ż, rz żaba, rzeka [ʒ] j de jour mais le point d'articulation est plus reculé. Le son est plus sombre et plus « épais ». masaż, kalendarz [ʂ] ch de chemin, mais plus dur et articulé plus en arrière dans la bouche sz szef dż dżem [d͡ʒ] proche du j français, mais précédée d'un très bref d, comme g de gelato en italian cz czas [t͡ʂ]] le tch français dans tchao, mais avec la langue légèrement plus en arrière dans la bouche ź źle [ʑ] ź est proche du j français dans je, mais plus doux et prononcé plus en avant dans la bouche. znaleźć [ɕ] ś est le correspondant sourd de ź. Il est proche du ch français dans chien, mais plus doux et prononcé plus en avant. ś świat dź dźwig [ʥ] dź est proche du dj dans adieu, mais plus doux et prononcé plus en avant. miedź [ʨ] ć est le correspondant sourde de dź. Il est proche du tch français, mais plus doux et prononcé plus en avant dans la bouche. ć ćma h, ch charakter, hotel [x] h et ch se prononcent de la même manière. Elles s'articulent à peu près au même endroit que le r français dans des mots comme carte ou tarte, mais sans faire vibrer la gorge. Il s'agit simplement d'un souffle produit à l'arrière de la bouche. r rdza [r] r se prononce en faisant vibrer la pointe de la langue juste derrière les dents supérieures

Source: Wikibooks – Polnisch/Kurs/Phonetik (translated and adapted).

docs.title: O alfabeto polonês
docs.text:
O alfabeto polonês baseia-se no alfabeto latino, mas possui 32 letras. Além de algumas letras que não são usadas em polonês (Q, V, X), inclui também várias letras próprias da língua polonesa.

O alfabeto polonês moderno é o seguinte:

Aa Ąą Bb Cc Ćć Dd Ee Ęę Ff Gg Hh Ii Jj Kk Ll Łł Mm Nn Ńń Oo Óó Pp Rr Ss Śś Tt Uu Ww Yy Zz Źź Żż

O pequeno sinal sob as letras ą e ę chama-se ogonek (em polonês: “rabinho”).

Além das letras simples, o polonês também possui vários dígrafos (duas letras que representam um único som):

ch, cz, dz, dź, dż, rz, sz

As letras Q, V e X não fazem parte do alfabeto polonês. Aparecem apenas em algumas abreviaturas (por exemplo, V para volt, em polonês wolt) ou em algumas palavras de origem estrangeira (por exemplo, taxi, quiz).

docs.title: Acentuação
docs.text:
Ao contrário do português, em que a posição da sílaba tônica varia, em polonês o acento tônico recai, em (quase) todos os casos, sobre a penúltima sílaba.

As exceções em que o acento recai sobre a antepenúltima sílaba (a terceira a contar do fim) incluem:

  • Empréstimos de origem grega terminados em -ika e -yka (fizyka [ˈfʲizɨka])
  • Verbos no passado com as terminações -śmy e -ście (pytaliście [pɨˈtalʲiɕʨɛ] em vez de [pɨtaˈlʲiɕʨɛ])
  • Verbos no condicional com as terminações -bym, -byś e -by (robiłbym [ˈrɔbʲiwbɨm] em vez de [rɔˈbʲiwbɨm])
  • Numerais (czterysta [ˈʧtɛrɨsta] em vez de [ʧtɛˈrɨsta])
  • Numerais seguidos do sufixo -kroć (tysiąckroć [ˈtɨɕɔnʦkrɔʨ] em vez de [tɨˈɕɔnʦkrɔʨ])

As exceções em que o acento recai sobre a quarta sílaba a contar do fim incluem:

  • Verbos no condicional com as terminações -byśmy e -byście (pisalibyśmy [pʲiˈsalʲibɨɕmɨ] em vez de [pʲisalʲiˈbɨɕmɨ])
  • Verbos no passado com as terminações -żeśmy e -żeście (spytaliżeście [spɨˈtalʲiʒɛɕʨɛ] em vez de [spɨtalʲiˈʒɛɕʨɛ])

docs.title: As vogais
docs.text:
As vogais polonesas são pronunciadas de forma curta, sem alongamento.

AFI Letra Exemplo escrito Exemplo de áudio Aproximação em português [a] a tak como o a de pá, curto e claro [ɛ] e krew como o é aberto de pé [i] i i como o i de vida [ɔ] o oko como o ó aberto de porta [u] ó, u mówić, ku como o u de tu [ɨ] y syn Não há equivalente exato no português brasileiro. No português europeu, aproxima-se do e átono em palavras como de. É produzido mais atrás na boca do que i e com a língua mais relaxada. [ɔ̃] ą mąż o nasal, aproximadamente como em bom, mas geralmente mais aberto [ɛ̃] ę język e nasal; não há equivalente exato, mas pode lembrar o início da vogal nasal em bem

Ao soletrar uma palavra, as letras a, e, i e o são simplesmente chamadas pelo próprio som.

Já as letras ó e u são ambas pronunciadas [u]. Para distingui-las ao soletrar, usam-se os nomes:

  • ó: u zamknięte (“u fechado”)
  • u: u otwarte (“u aberto”)

Também se usam outros nomes para ó:

  • o kreskowane (“o com traço”)
  • o z kreską (“o com um traço”)

A escolha entre ó e u é essencialmente etimológica (ligada à história da palavra). Por isso, é uma das dificuldades ortográficas mais frequentes em polonês.

A letra y chama-se igrek [ˈigrɛk] (nome historicamente derivado da expressão francesa para “i grego”). Entre todas as vogais polonesas, y é a única que nunca pode aparecer no início de uma palavra.

docs.title: As consoantes e a letra i
docs.text:
Em polonês, a letra i colocada depois de uma consoante pode palatalizá-la (isto é, torná-la “suave”, aproximando a língua do palato).

Quando uma vogal vem depois de i, esse i pode servir apenas para indicar a palatalização da consoante anterior.

O i antes de uma vogal:

  • depois das letras c, s, z, dz e n, não é pronunciado como uma vogal separada;
  • depois de outras consoantes, geralmente acrescenta uma passagem semelhante a [j], como o som de i em português em sequências como iate.

Assim, as consoantes palatais ć, ś, ź, dź e ń escrevem-se:

  • ć, ś, ź, dź, ń antes de uma consoante ou no fim de uma palavra;
  • ci, si, zi, dzi, ni antes de uma vogal.
Letras AFI Exemplo escrito Exemplo de áudio Observações bi [bʲ] biały pi [pʲ] piasek gi [gʲ] ogień ki [kʲ] cukier wi [wʲ] wiatr fi [fʲ] geografia di [dʲ] diabeł dzi [ʥ] dziad equivalente a dź ti [tʲ] sympatia ci [ʨ] ciasto equivalente a ć zi [ʑ] zielony equivalente a ź si [ɕ] siarka equivalente a ś hi [çʲ] hiena li [lʲ] afiliacja mi [mʲ] anatomia ni [ɲ] kuchnia equivalente a ń; muito próximo de nh em português ria [rʲ] abituria

Observe que as consoantes suaves nunca podem preceder y, e as consoantes duras quase nunca precedem i. (Exceções: empréstimos lexicais, por exemplo dżinsy [ˈʤinsɨ] = jeans.)

docs.title: Vogais nasais
docs.text:
As letras ę e ą representam vogais nasais: ę parte de um e nasal e ą de um o nasal. A pronúncia concreta depende fortemente da consoante seguinte.

Letra Consoante seguinte Exemplo escrito AFI Exemplo de áudio Aproximação em português ą f, w, h, ch, s, z, sz, ż, rz, ś, ź, fim de palavra mąż [ɔ̃] vogal nasal semelhante a um o nasal português, mas geralmente mais aberta b, p skąpiec [ɔm] aproxima-se de om: a nasalidade realiza-se como m antes de b/p g, k pociąg [ɔŋ] aproxima-se de ong, com som nasal [ŋ], como o ng inglês de sing c, dz, d, t, cz, dż piątek [ɔn] aproxima-se de on, com um n claramente articulado ć, dź bądź [ɔɲ] aproxima-se de oń; o som nasal final é semelhante ao nh português ę f, w, h, ch, s, z, sz, ż, rz, ś, ź język [ɛ̃] aproxima-se de em b, p gęba [ɛm] aproxima-se de em: a nasalidade realiza-se como m antes de b/p g, k dźwięk [ɛŋ] aproxima-se de eng, com som nasal [ŋ], como o ng inglês de sing c, dz, d, t, cz, dż wędrować [ɛn] aproxima-se de en, com um n claramente articulado ć, dź wszędzie [ɛɲ] aproxima-se de eń; o som nasal final é semelhante ao nh português fim da palavra imię [ɛ] no fim da palavra, normalmente soa como um e polonês comum, sem nasalização forte

docs.title: Consoantes “simples”
docs.text:
Começamos pelas consoantes que têm equivalentes próximos em português. No fim de uma palavra ou antes de uma consoante surda, as consoantes sonoras que possuem um par surdo passam a ser pronunciadas como esse par surdo.

Letra Exemplo escrito Exemplo de áudio AFI Aproximação em português b bardzo [b] como b em bem chleb [p] como p em pai p pan d dom [d] como d em dar (sem a palatalização que pode ocorrer no português brasileiro antes de i) kod [t] como t em tarde (sem palatalização) t tak g góra [g] como g em gato katalog [k] como c em casa k kod w waga [v] como v em vaca staw [f] como f em faca f fala z za [z] como z em zero raz [s] como s em sapo s sam j jajo [j] como a semivogal [j] no início de iate l lato [l] como l em lado; em polonês mantém-se [l] também no fim da sílaba m moment [m] como m em mão n noga [n] como n em nada ń koń [ɲ] como nh em vinho ł łuk [w] como a semivogal [w], semelhante ao u em quase

docs.title: Consoantes sem equivalente exato em português
docs.text:
A seguir vêm consoantes que não têm um equivalente exato em português. Aqui também, no fim de uma palavra ou antes de uma consoante surda, as consoantes sonoras que possuem um par surdo passam a ser pronunciadas como esse par surdo.

Letra Exemplo escrito Exemplo de áudio AFI Rémarques dz dzwon [dz] dz é uma africada: pronuncie d + z num único movimento, sem separar os dois sons. ksiądz [ts] c soa como ts pronunciado num único movimento, como no início de tsunami. É o correspondente surdo de dz. c cena ż, rz żaba, rzeka [ʒ] lembra o som de j em jogo, mas é articulado mais atrás na boca e soa mais “escuro” e espesso masaż, kalendarz [ʂ] lembra o som de ch em chave, mas é articulado mais atrás na boca e soa mais duro sz szef dż dżem [d͡ʒ] uma africada sonora: começa com um d muito breve e passa imediatamente para um som semelhante ao j de jogo, mas com a língua mais atrás cz czas [t͡ʂ]] soa aproximadamente como tch em tchau, mas com a língua ligeiramente mais atrás na boca ź źle [ʑ] ź lembra um j muito suave, mas é pronunciado mais à frente, com a língua próxima do palato; não há equivalente exato em português znaleźć [ɕ] ś é o correspondente surdo de ź. Lembra um ch muito suave, pronunciado mais à frente e com a língua próxima do palato. ś świat dź dźwig [ʥ] dź é uma africada muito suave: começa com d e passa imediatamente para um som palatal semelhante a ź; não há equivalente exato em português miedź [ʨ] ć é o correspondente surdo de dź. Lembra tch, mas é muito mais suave e pronunciado mais à frente, com a língua próxima do palato. ć ćma h, ch charakter, hotel [x] h e ch pronunciam-se da mesma maneira. O som [x] é produzido com uma fricção na parte de trás da boca, semelhante ao j do espanhol jamón. Em algumas variedades do português, pode lembrar uma realização forte de r, mas sem vibração. r rdza [r] r é vibrado com a ponta da língua logo atrás dos dentes superiores, semelhante ao rr vibrante de algumas variedades do português ou ao r do espanhol.

Fonte: Wikibooks – Polnisch/Kurs/Phonetik (traduzido e adaptado).
